title: Farage Defends £72m Donations as Parliament Debates Cap
summary:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has said two big donations given to his party are "100% compliant with the law today," but was not able to say whether they would be permissible if a rule change, currently being debated in Parliament, were passed. Ministers are seeking to put a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British expats, backdated to 25 March 2026. Farage argued the government should not retrospectively declare donations illegal and threatened to retaliate by limiting trade union donations, if elected PM.

Over the weekend, Reform announced that it had received two donations of £36m each from wealthy businessmen Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British but have until recently lived abroad. Asked if the two men were resident in the UK by 25 March, Farage said: "I'm not going into their particular details." He went on to criticise the government's attempts to retrospectively declare some donations illegal, saying: "This cannot be."

"If the government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There would be a response the other way," Farage said. "We or the Conservatives would say 'if you're going to stop legitimate donors like this, we would say to the trade unions, you can't give money'." Farage argued such a move would "collapse" the system of political funding and lead to taxpayers having to fund political parties, a system he said would be opposed by the British public.

Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees. Trade union leader Paul Nowak said there was no similarity between "care workers chipping in a few quid a year through their union and a party bought and paid for by billionaires."

The House of Lords is currently debating the government's Representation of the People Bill which caps the amount British people living overseas can donate to political parties at £100,000. The bill also states that those who moved back to the UK would have to wait for at least a year before donating more than £100,000. The legislation states that donors must have been registered as in the UK by 25 March 2026 in order to avoid the cap. It is not currently clear exactly when Delo and Harborne returned to the UK. The new rule changes had been added to the bill, following a report by former senior civil servant Sir Philip Rycroft into foreign interference in British politics, published on 25 March.
why_it_matters: Rules about political money decide who gets to shape elections and whose voice is loudest, and this debate exposes the tension between closing loopholes and letting parties fund themselves freely — an argument playing out in many democracies, not just Britain.

background_read: Reform UK (a right-wing populist party that grew out of the Brexit Party and is led by Nigel Farage) won a large share of the vote in the 2024 general election but only a handful of seats, because Britain's first-past-the-post system rewards concentrated support rather than a spread-out share.

The House of Lords, where the Representation of the People Bill is being debated, is the unelected upper chamber of the UK Parliament; it reviews and can amend bills but does not have the final say, which lies with the elected House of Commons.

UK political funding is policed by the Electoral Commission, an independent regulator, and the law requires donors to be on the UK electoral register. British citizens living abroad have historically been allowed to keep that voting right for a limited time, which created the loophole that the new residency rule is meant to close.

Trade unions have funded the Labour Party since it was founded with union support more than a century ago, and members' small membership fees are pooled into those donations — the contrast Labour's critics make with a handful of billionaire donors.

Sir Philip Rycroft (a former senior civil servant and one of the UK's top officials during the Brexit years) published a government review on foreign interference in British politics, and the residency cap was added to the bill in response to his findings.

perspectives.description: Farage argues the donations broke no existing rule and that changing the law retrospectively to cancel them would be unfair and politically dangerous. In his view, tighter limits would only push parties toward taxpayer funding that the public would resent.

Ministers and union leader Paul Nowak say a handful of billionaires should not be able to buy influence, especially when they have only recently returned from living abroad. They frame the cap as a defence against foreign interference, and reject the comparison with millions of union members paying small fees.

Every democracy struggles with where to draw the line between free political speech and undue influence, and the UK depends heavily on private donations with no spending ceiling. Backdating a cap is unusual because it changes the rules mid-game, which is why the residency dates of the two donors have become the crux of the dispute.

If the bill passes as written, parties will have to vet donors' residency far more carefully, and any future large gifts from abroad become far harder to accept. Farage's threat to hit union funding shows the fight could escalate into a wider remaking of how British politics is paid for.
